claims.text: The starting coating consists of sputter-deposited, alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers with individual layer thicknesses of 5–20 nm.
The as-deposited multilayer has appreciable chemical short-range order within each layer and well-defined interfaces.
Compositional complexity and processing conditions induce short-range order in the multilayer.
Progressive creep in nanoscale FCC/BCC HEA multilayers is governed by the evolution and local breakdown of SRO at interfaces and within layers.
Initial SRO pins dislocations and limits plastic flow.
Mechanical loading can cause a local, diffusionless rearrangement of short-range order.
The mechanically driven rearrangement constitutes partial degradation or breakdown of SRO.
SRO breakdown locally softens the lattice by reducing the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation and glide.
SRO breakdown activates additional dislocation slip and climb.
Local SRO breakdown progressively increases dislocation density and mobility, producing creep deformation.
SRO breakdown is a precursor to accelerated creep.
A mild post-deposition anneal can increase the degree of SRO relative to the as-deposited state.
An annealed, higher-SRO multilayer should initially have a lower creep strain rate than the as-deposited baseline.
The higher-SRO sample should undergo a distinct transition to faster creep after local SRO breakdown.
The accelerated-creep transition should be accompanied by localized slip bands or twins that are absent or less pronounced in the baseline.
The as-deposited baseline has moderate SRO and undergoes conventional dislocation-mediated plasticity during sustained loading.
The hypothesis is restricted to conditions that preserve the multilayer architecture, phase stability, and nanoscale interface integrity.
The applicable regime requires enough temperature and stress to drive SRO evolution without causing substantial interdiffusion or complete phase transformation.

An absence of systematic differences in accelerated-creep onset, SRO breakdown, and dislocation-structure evolution between annealed and as-deposited samples would falsify the proposed SRO-controlled mechanism.
